lane.name: Post-punk and noise rock
lane.definition: Wire, Mission of Burma, Big Black, Fugazi, and modern post-punk like Robber Robber: the rhythmic, angular line adjacent to the scene.

albums.label: Harvest Records
albums.description: Wire strip punk down to blunt, angular fragments — 21 songs in under 36 minutes, several barely a minute long — replacing Ramones-style buzz with clipped riffs, deadpan vocals and abrupt stops. It is the founding document of art-punk's move into post-punk, endlessly cited by Minor Threat, R.E.M. and Elastica alike. The essential landmark for the rhythmic, angular line adjacent to the scene.
albums.lineage: Splits off V29's art-punk deadpan and the punk foundation of X14 into a more clipped, structurally radical post-punk; its influence runs forward through Minor Threat and Fugazi's DIY rigor rather than toward twang or country.

albums.label: Harvest Records
albums.description: Wire's second album opens up the terse songs of Pink Flag into longer, synth-and-effects-laden arrangements, edging toward the atmospheric side of post-punk without losing its angularity. It shows the band already restless with the sound they had just invented. A strong second landmark for hearing post-punk's rapid evolution.
albums.lineage: Continues Wire's branch off X14/V29 into more textured, synth-inflected post-punk; its atmosphere influenced the goth and art-rock wings of the genre rather than the twangier Core lineage.

albums.label: Harvest Records
albums.description: Named for the number of shows the band had played, 154 pushes furthest into studio experimentation and melodic ambition before Wire's late-70s lineup fractured. It closes out the trilogy that made Pink Flag, Chairs Missing and 154 foundational post-punk texts. A deeper cut for listeners already sold on the first two records.
albums.lineage: The final entry in Wire's initial branch off X14/V29's post-punk lineage before a long hiatus; its polish anticipated 80s art-rock production more than the DIY roughness that fed the American noise-rock wing.

albums.label: Ace of Hearts Records
albums.description: Mission of Burma's only studio album from their original run pairs blaring, tape-loop-treated guitar squall with tightly wound rhythms and Roger Miller and Clint Conley's alternating shouted vocals. It is a foundational text for American noise-rock and post-hardcore. Essential for the angular, rhythmic line that runs from Boston's scene through Fugazi and beyond.
albums.lineage: An American, Boston-scene branch off X14's punk foundation and V29's art-noise lineage; its tape-loop noise and structural aggression sound like groundwork for the noise-rock wing of X10 rather than any twang-adjacent lane.
key_tracks: That's When I Reach for My Revolver

albums.label: Homestead Records
albums.description: Steve Albini's Big Black replace a drummer with a programmed Roland drum machine and pair it with clanging, treated guitars and confrontational lyrics about violence and small-town rot. Atomizer is the genre-defining noise-rock record, mechanical and abrasive where Mission of Burma is loose and shouted. A must-hear landmark for the harder, industrial-adjacent end of the post-punk/noise-rock line.
albums.lineage: Splits from X14's hardcore roots into a colder, drum-machine-driven noise rock distinct from Wire or Mission of Burma's more melodic post-punk; Albini's engineering work afterward directly shaped the Pixies, Nirvana and much of 90s indie production.

albums.label: Touch and Go Records
albums.description: Big Black's second and final studio album sharpens Atomizer's clanging drum-machine noise rock with even more caustic production and a cover of Kraftwerk's 'The Model' rendered as pure menace. It closed out the band before Albini moved fully into producing other artists' records. A strong second landmark for the noise-rock wing of the lane.
albums.lineage: The endpoint of Big Black's branch off X14's punk lineage before Albini's influence shifted from performing to producing; its scorched-earth sound directly informed Shellac and the broader 90s noise-rock underground.

albums.label: Dischord Records
albums.description: Fugazi's first full-length turns Ian MacKaye's hardcore background and Guy Picciotto's more melodic instincts into tense, dub-influenced post-hardcore built on stop-start dynamics and pointedly political lyrics. Repeater made the band's DIY ethics (five-dollar shows, no merch) as influential as its music. The essential landmark for the DIY-network end of the rhythmic, angular line.
albums.lineage: Grows out of X14's hardcore-punk roots (MacKaye's earlier Minor Threat) with an art-rock structural sense that recalls V29; Fugazi's DIY model became a touchstone for the independent touring network that runs into lo-fi indie and the Core.

albums.label: Dischord Records
albums.description: A heavier, more abrasive record than Repeater, In on the Kill Taker came together after the band shelved early sessions with Steve Albini and finished it on their own terms. It holds some of Fugazi's most aggressive material and shows the post-hardcore/noise-rock overlap within the lane at its most direct. A strong second landmark for the band's catalog.
albums.lineage: Continues Fugazi's post-hardcore branch, with abandoned Albini sessions brushing it against the noise-rock wing of the same lane; its aggression seems to have shaped 90s post-hardcore more than any twang-adjacent lineage.

albums.label: Dischord Records
albums.description: Fugazi loosen their sound on Red Medicine, adding studio experimentation, instrumental detours and quieter passages alongside the usual tense dynamics, self-produced entirely on their own terms. It shows a band expanding past hardcore's constraints while keeping its DIY politics intact. Recommended for hearing the band's mid-career evolution.
albums.lineage: A later, more experimental branch off Fugazi's X14/V29 post-hardcore lineage; its loosened structure anticipated post-rock's use of dynamics more than it fed back toward the lane's noisier origins.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: Reuniting after a 20-year hiatus, Mission of Burma sound barely diminished on ONoffON, matching Vs.'s aggression with slightly cleaner production and Bob Weston (of Shellac) replacing original tape-loop manipulator Martin Swope. It proved the band's reunion was substance over nostalgia. A useful modern example of the lane's founders still working.
albums.lineage: A late-career continuation of Mission of Burma's original branch off X14/V29's noise-punk lineage, with a Shellac/Big Black connection tying it to the Chicago noise-rock wing of the same lane.

albums.label: Hardly Art
albums.description: Joe Casey's world-weary, half-spoken baritone narrates Rust Belt decay and municipal corruption over Greg Ahee's needling, repetitive guitar lines, updating Wire and Fall-style post-punk for post-recession Detroit. It is the modern touchstone for the lane's angular, rhythmic vocabulary translated into American indie rock. A good example of a current band still working directly in Wire's tradition.
albums.lineage: A modern American continuation of the post-punk branch off X14/V29, closer to the Fall's deadpan delivery than to noise rock's abrasiveness; feeds today's post-punk revival (Idles, Shame) rather than the Core's twang.

albums.label: Domino
albums.description: Protomartyr's fourth album widens its scope to post-truth politics and mortality, with Casey's lyrics sharper and the band's arrangements more expansive than on earlier records. Ahee's guitars shift between spindly patterns and heavy surges under the baritone narration. Recommended as a second, more polished entry point.
albums.lineage: Continues Protomartyr's modern post-punk branch off X14/V29; its political storytelling parallels Southern-gothic songwriting elsewhere in the atlas without ever crossing into twang.

albums.label: Saddle Creek
albums.description: Indigo De Souza's second album swings between shredded-throat pop-punk catharsis and glossy synth interludes, with songs about grief, queerness and self-destruction delivered with disarming directness. She is placed here on a scene-not-sound ruling: she is a central figure of the Asheville DIY community that also produced MJ Lenderman and Wednesday, but her sound is punk/pop-punk rather than countrygaze. Included as a Context landmark for that Asheville connective tissue.
albums.lineage: Not a sonic descendant of the post-punk canon above; included in X10 because her music runs angular and punk-adjacent rather than twangy, and because she shares the Asheville scene (not the sound) with Core artists like Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

albums.label: Fire Talk Records
albums.description: Robber Robber's Fire Talk debut hits harder and more explosively than the Burlington quartet's earlier work, pairing thick, distorted guitars with tightly coiled, start-stop arrangements closer to noise rock than to twang. They are placed here on a scene-not-sound ruling, tying them to Vermont's small but tight-knit DIY guitar-band scene. A modern example rounding out the lane's contemporary edge.
albums.lineage: Not a direct sonic descendant of classic post-punk; included in X10 because their noisy, angular guitar rock fits the lane's sound while their real connection to the wider atlas is scene (Burlington, VT DIY) rather than genre lineage into twang.
